answer_text:
# Evaluating the Limit

## Setting Up the Expression

The sum can be recognized as an expectation. Let $K \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)$. Then:

$$\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} e^{-2ck} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{-2cK}\right]$$

## Applying the Binomial Theorem

I can factor $e^{-2ck}$ into the summand:

$$\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}\underbrace{p^k e^{-2ck}}_{(pe^{-2c})^k}(1-p)^{n-k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(pe^{-2c})^k(1-p)^{n-k}$$

By the binomial theorem, this collapses to:

$$\big(pe^{-2c} + (1-p)\big)^n = \big(1 - p + pe^{-2c}\big)^n = \big(1 - p(1 - e^{-2c})\big)^n$$

## Analyzing the Limit

Since $c > 0$, we have $0 < e^{-2c} < 1$, so:
$$1 - e^{-2c} > 0$$

Since $0 < p < 1$, we have:
$$0 < p(1 - e^{-2c}) < 1$$

Therefore the base satisfies:
$$0 < 1 - p(1 - e^{-2c}) < 1$$

A number strictly between $0$ and $1$, raised to the $n$-th power, converges to $0$:

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\big(1 - p(1 - e^{-2c})\big)^n = 0$$

## Verification (Concrete Example)

For $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$, $c = 1$: the base is $\frac{1+e^{-2}}{2} \approx 0.5677$, and $(0.5677)^n \to 0$. ✓

## Conclusion

The limit equals $0$, so the equation **does hold**.

$$\boxed{0}$$
